summary: Describes a proposed URN namespace to be managed by DANTE, for naming persistent resources defined by GEANT, the consortium of European academic and research networks, and its projects, activities, and working groups. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Research groups in Europe need stable, unique names for their documents. This note sets up a name family for them.

questions: what is the geant urn namespace
what is a persistent resource identifier
subtitle: Stable names for resources across European research networks

tldr.problem: GEANT, a coalition of European research and education networks, creates many documents, specifications, schemas, and other resources. They need stable, globally unique identifiers for these resources that will not change even if the documents move to different servers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a URN (Uniform Resource Name) namespace with the prefix 'urn:geant:' that DANTE (the organization operating GEANT) manages. Resources are named hierarchically using colon-separated tokens, with the leftmost part typically identifying the NREN (National Research and Education Network) or GEANT working group responsible for that resource.
tldr.outcome: GEANT communities can assign persistent names to their resources without coordination with a central registry, by delegating naming authority to subordinate organizations, each of which guarantees uniqueness within their branch.

today: RFC 4926 registered the 'geant' URN namespace with IANA. The namespace remains active and available for GEANT community use. However, as of 2024, the GEANT consortium has evolved through multiple generations (GEANT, GEANT2, GEANT3, GEANT4), and the adoption of this URN namespace by GEANT projects appears limited. The principles of the RFC remain sound: institutions needing persistent, decentralized resource identifiers can use similar approaches.

sections.title: GEANT and the Need for Persistent Identifiers
sections.content:
GEANT is a consortium of European academic and research networks. It provides high-speed network connectivity and infrastructure for universities and research institutions across Europe. The network evolved over nearly two decades, with each generation improving capability.

GEANT is operated by DANTE, a UK-based organization, and is funded through EU projects, the largest of which is the GN2 project. The GEANT community produces many kinds of documents: technical specifications, working drafts, project reports, XML schemas, stylesheets, and policy documents.

The problem: these resources need globally unique, persistent identifiers that do not change, even if the resource moves to a new server or location. A persistent identifier stays the same for decades, allowing external documents to cite it and rely on finding the same resource. The RFC proposes a URN (Uniform Resource Name) namespace specifically for GEANT resources to solve this problem.
sections.eli5: Researchers in Europe make lots of documents. They want to give each one a number that always means the same thing, so it can be cited forever, even if the document gets moved to a new website.

sections.title: What is a URN and How It Works
sections.content:
A URN (Uniform Resource Name) is an identifier that names something without saying where it is. Unlike a URL (like http://example.com/doc.pdf), which tells you the exact location, a URN is location-independent. A URN has the form urn:namespace:identifier.

For GEANT resources, the format is urn:geant:identifier. The geant part is the Namespace ID (NID), unique to GEANT. Everything after the colon is the Namespace Specific String (NSS), which identifies the particular resource.

The NSS consists of colon-separated tokens, forming a hierarchy. For example, a working group might use urn:geant:dfn.de:schema:example, where dfn.de (the German National Research and Education Network) is responsible for everything under that prefix, and schema and example are further subdivisions.
sections.eli5: A URN is a name, not an address. Instead of 'go to this website', it says 'I'm the GEANT thing called dfn.de:schema:example'. A resolution service can look it up if needed, but the name never changes.

sections.title: Hierarchical Naming and Authority Delegation
sections.content:
The key to making URN namespaces work at scale is delegation. DANTE manages the top level of the GEANT namespace and assigns subordinate naming authorities (such as the German NREN, the French NREN, and so on). Each subordinate naming authority is responsible for assigning names within their portion of the tree and for granting naming authority to further subordinates if needed.

To guarantee uniqueness, DANTE requires that immediately subordinate naming authorities use lowercase only, preventing accidental registration of two authorities whose names differ only in case. Institutions seeking GEANT affiliation can propose to be designated a subordinate naming authority by sending email to geant-submit@dante.org.uk.

Each subordinate naming authority inherits the responsibility for maintaining the usability of URNs in their branch. DANTE enforces this by contacting liaisons from each subordinate authority on at least an annual basis. If there is no response or the liaison indicates the authority should lapse, DANTE reclaims control of that branch. This ensures that naming authority is never abandoned for more than one year.
sections.eli5: DANTE says 'German NREN, you manage urn:geant:dfn.de:*'. The German NREN can then say 'department X, you manage urn:geant:dfn.de:dept-x:*'. Everyone guarantees unique names in their part.

sections.title: Resolution and Validation
sections.content:
While a URN is a name independent of location, users often want to find the actual resource. DANTE maintains an index of GEANT-assigned URNs on its website (http://www.dante.net/urn-geant/urn-geant.html) that maps URNs to URLs or other resource identifiers. This index allows a tool or person to resolve a URN to a concrete location.

Subordinate naming authorities can define their own resolution services for URNs they assign. The RFC specifies that presence in DANTE's index implies validity: if a URN is listed, it is valid.

Conformance is straightforward: all GEANT URNs fully conform to the standard URN syntax defined in RFC 2141. This means they can be used anywhere URN syntax is expected, ensuring broad compatibility.
sections.eli5: The name itself doesn't change, but there's a registry that says 'urn:geant:dfn.de:doc1 is at http://example.org/doc1.pdf'. If you look up the URN, you find the actual document.

sections.title: Justification and Community Use
sections.content:
GEANT considered using existing URN namespaces (like XMLORG or OASIS) but determined that creating a dedicated namespace was justified. GEANT needs autonomy in naming: it is not a member of OASIS, so becoming a subordinate under OASIS would be awkward. GEANT also names non-XML resources (schemas are just one category), so general-purpose XML namespaces were not ideal.

The RFC notes that a single resource could have multiple URNs: a GEANT-created schema could later be registered with XMLORG and receive an XMLORG URN without losing its GEANT URN. Both would point to the same resource.

It is expected that after the namespace is established, GEANT will develop a distributed resolution service (similar to other pan-European services like EduROAM and PerfSONAR) to make URN lookup fast and reliable across the continent.
sections.eli5: GEANT needs its own namespace, not because others don't exist, but because GEANT wants to manage its own names and isn't part of those other systems. Over time, they will build tools to look up the names quickly.
